warmup.q: A Redis sorted set (a type that keeps its items in order by a number) holds 128 shops with short names. Redis's MEMORY USAGE command says the key takes about 1 KB. You add one more shop with a short name. What happens to its memory?
options: It grows by a few bytes, the size of one more entry
It grows about tenfold, to around 11 KB
Nothing changes until the set reaches 512 members
Redis refuses to add it until you raise a memory setting
warmup.why: Up to 128 members, Redis packs a sorted set into one compact block of memory called a listpack. The 129th member crosses the default limit, zset-max-listpack-entries (128), and Redis rebuilds the key as a hash table plus a skip list, with links and a separate piece of memory for every member. On the lab server, MEMORY USAGE went from 1,076 to 10,888 bytes. The first option is the trap, because it's how a list in your own program seems to grow. 512 is the limit for hashes and for sets of whole numbers, not for sorted sets. This lesson builds up why: in a store that lives in memory, the bookkeeping around small items decides how much fits.

sections.h: Five types for five jobs in the payments app
sections.html:
Let's start with the jobs. The payments app keeps five kinds of data in Redis, and each kind fits one of its types. Inside an in-memory store named them; here's what each one is for.

A count of today's payments is a number you add to. Redis keeps it in a string, its basic value: any bytes, up to 512 MB. When the bytes are a whole number, INCR and DECRBY do the arithmetic on the server.

A payment record has fields: status, amount, currency. With only strings, you'd store it as one JSON string (text in a common format for structured data) and rewrite all of it to change the status. That's read, change, write back: the race from Inside an in-memory store. Or you'd keep one key per field and pay a round trip, a message to Redis and its answer back, for each. A hash is a small map of fields inside one key. HSET payment:43 status settled changes one field on the server, and HGETALL reads them all in one round trip.

Every night, the company pays each shop what it took, in batches that wait in line for a worker program. They need order: first in, first out. A list keeps items in the order they were added, and it's cheap at both ends. RPUSH adds at the tail, and LPOP takes from the head. The lab calls this queue settlement:queue, after the trade's word for paying the shops. (A lighter log: Redis pub/sub and Streams, in the Messaging and logs track, shows why Streams make a better queue.)

The cards the fraud team flagged today need membership: is this card in the group or not? A set holds unique members, so adding a member twice changes nothing. SADD adds, and SISMEMBER checks.

Shops ranked by approved payments need order by a number that keeps changing. A sorted set holds unique members, each with a number called its score, and keeps them sorted by score. ZINCRBY raises a score, and ZRANGE reads the top ten.

Cost matters as much as shape, because every command runs on that one thread. Redis writes costs in Big-O notation, where N is the number of items in the key. O(1) means the work doesn't grow with the key. O(N) means it grows in step with it: twice the items, twice the work. O(log N) grows very slowly, since doubling N adds only one step. M is the number of items a command returns.

Type Example key Main commands Cost
string card:7:status, auths:today GET, SET, INCR O(1)
hash payment:43 HGET, HSET, HINCRBY O(1) per field, HGETALL O(N)
list settlement:queue RPUSH, LPOP, LRANGE O(1) at either end
set fraud:flagged SADD, SISMEMBER, SINTER O(1) add and check, SMEMBERS O(N)
sorted set merchants:approved ZADD, ZINCRBY, ZRANGE O(log N), ranges O(log N + M)

Key names are plain strings. The habit is type:id with colons, such as payment:43 or merchant:m-17:approved. Redis doesn't care, but a shared start lets the command SCAN MATCH payment:* find a whole family of keys, and your teammates can read it.

That's the outside of each type. Next, we'll see how Redis lays them out in memory, and why a small key looks different inside.

try.title: Use each type once
steps: Start the server if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d from the labs folder; Docker runs it in a container). Then open Redis's prompt with docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli.
Type the commands below, one at a time. Before each one, say what it will print.
Predict the last one: what happens when you GET a hash?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SET card:7:status active
HSET payment:43 status approved amount 1250 currency EUR
RPUSH settlement:queue batch-1 batch-2 batch-3
LPOP settlement:queue
SADD fraud:flagged card:7 card:9 card:7
SCARD fraud:flagged
SISMEMBER fraud:flagged card:9
ZADD merchants:approved 42 m-17 40 m-03 12 m-88
ZRANGE merchants:approved 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
TYPE settlement:queue
GET payment:43

try.expect: RPUSH returns the new length, (integer) 3, and LPOP hands back "batch-1", the oldest entry. SADD returns (integer) 2: the second card:7 was already there, so SCARD, the count of members, says 2. SISMEMBER returns (integer) 1, meaning yes. ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES lists m-17 42, m-03 40, m-88 12, highest first. TYPE settlement:queue says list. GET payment:43 fails with (error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value: GET is a command for strings, and the key holds a hash.

sections.h: Small keys are packed into one block, big ones become a hash table or a skip list
sections.html:
Picture a hash with three fields, stored the way Java's HashMap, a hash table, stores its entries. There's a table of slots, one entry object per field, and a separate piece of memory for each field and each value. They're joined by pointers, 8-byte memory addresses that say where the next piece lives. Every piece of memory a program asks for also carries a small header. For status approved amount 1250 currency EUR, 35 bytes of real data, the bookkeeping weighs more than the data. Multiply by ten million payment records, and much of your RAM holds pointers.

The simplest fix is to drop the structure. Write the entries one after another into a single block of memory, each with its length in front, and find a field by reading from the start. That's a listpack, and it's the owner's notebook page from the opening. On the lab server, the three-field hash took 77 bytes as a listpack and 215 bytes as a hash table. The price is the search: finding a field means walking the block, which is O(N). For a hundred short entries in about a kilobyte, the walk is cheap, because the CPU reads bytes that sit side by side very fast.

Where does it break? At size. Walking 10,000 entries on every HGET (a read of one field), on the one thread every client shares, is too slow. And adding an entry in the middle of a big block means moving every byte after it. So Redis uses both layouts: a listpack while the key is small, and the general structure once it grows. TYPE still says hash. What changes is the encoding, the layout behind the type, which the command OBJECT ENCODING reports.

For a big hash or set, the general structure is a hash table. A big sorted set needs two things at once: find a member's score fast, and keep the members in score order. A sorted array would find positions fast, but adding a member would shift everything after it. A linked list, where each item points to the next, adds members cheaply, but finding the right place means walking it. So Redis keeps two structures holding the same members. A hash table maps each member to its score. A skip list keeps the members in score order: it's a linked list where some items carry extra links that jump far ahead, like express lanes. A search rides the top lane and drops down a lane whenever it would overshoot, so finding a position takes O(log N). That pair is the owner's box of cards and her ranked list on the wall.

Two more layouts complete the set. A set of plain whole numbers has its own compact form, the intset: a sorted array, searched by halving the range at each step. And a big list becomes a quicklist, a linked list of listpacks of up to 8 KB each.

These are the 8.10 defaults:

Setting Default Becomes
hash-max-listpack-entries and -value 512 fields, 64 bytes hashtable
set-max-intset-entries 512 integers hashtable
set-max-listpack-entries and -value 128 members, 64 bytes hashtable
zset-max-listpack-entries and -value 128 members, 64 bytes skiplist
list-max-listpack-size -2, meaning 8 KB quicklist

Either limit triggers the switch: too many entries, or one entry longer than the value limit. A single 65-byte member turns a two-member sorted set into a skip list. The switch goes one way only. Remove members until the key is tiny again, and it keeps the big encoding. That's where the notebook picture breaks: the owner can go back to one page when her list shrinks, and Redis never does. The switch costs memory, too. On the lab server, a sorted set of 128 short members took 1,076 bytes, and the 129th member made it 10,888.

Strings have encodings too: int for a whole number that fits in 64 bits, embstr for a short string kept in one piece of memory with its header, and raw for longer ones.

Encodings shrink what's inside a key. Every key also has a cost of its own, whatever it holds. Next, we'll weigh it.

frames.say: Remove the 129th member and the set is back to 128, but it stays a skip list, at 10,741 bytes. Redis converts up, never down. To get the compact form back, you'd rebuild the key, for example by copying the members into a new key that starts small.

try.title: Watch a sorted set change shape
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run the commands below one at a time. The first four ask how keys from the previous Try it are stored. The EVAL runs a tiny Lua script that adds 128 members in one go.
Before ZADD board 129 m-129, predict the encoding and the memory after it.
Before the last OBJECT ENCODING small, predict what one 65-character member does to a two-member set. (Paste 65 x's, or any 65-character string.)

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SET auths:today 41
OBJECT ENCODING auths:today
OBJECT ENCODING card:7:status
OBJECT ENCODING payment:43
EVAL "for i = 1, 128 do redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], i, 'm-' .. i) end" 1 board
OBJECT ENCODING board
MEMORY USAGE board
ZADD board 129 m-129
OBJECT ENCODING board
MEMORY USAGE board
ZREM board m-129
OBJECT ENCODING board
ZADD small 1 m-1
OBJECT ENCODING small
ZADD small 2 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
OBJECT ENCODING small
CONFIG GET zset-max-listpack-*

try.expect: auths:today is "int" (the value is a number, so Redis stores it as one), card:7:status is "embstr", and the three-field payment:43 is "listpack". With 128 members, board is "listpack" at (integer) 1076 bytes. After the 129th, it's "skiplist" at (integer) 10888, about ten times more. After ZREM, it's back to 128 members and still "skiplist". small starts as "listpack" and becomes "skiplist" with only two members, because one member is longer than 64 bytes. CONFIG GET shows the two limits: zset-max-listpack-entries 128 and zset-max-listpack-value 64. Byte counts can differ by a few percent between Redis builds.

sections.h: Every key pays a fixed cost in Redis's table of keys
sections.html:
Write 100,000 tiny keys into Redis 8.10, each a 10-byte name with the 4-byte value done, and its memory grows by about 55 bytes per key. Only about 14 of those bytes are your data. The rest is a cost every key pays, whatever it holds, because all the keys on a server live in one big hash table, the keyspace, from each key's name to its value. Caches mostly hold small items. In Twitter's study of 153 cache clusters, from Why caches work, the typical cluster's average key was under 38 bytes and its average value about 230 bytes. Memcached, an older cache program, spends 56 bytes of bookkeeping on every item. At those sizes, the fixed cost per key decides how many keys fit in RAM.

Here Redis and Valkey, a free copy of Redis that has gone its own way since 2024, differ. Redis 7.2, the version Valkey started from, keeps the keyspace in a chained hash table. That's an array of buckets (slots), each pointing to a separate entry, which points to the key and to the value. A lookup follows about four pointers, and each one can be a trip to RAM, the 100 ns rung from Why caches work. Valkey 8.1 replaced it with buckets of 64 bytes, the size of the piece the CPU loads from RAM at a time. A bucket holds up to seven entries, plus one byte of each entry's hash, a number worked out from the key's name. That one byte rules out almost every wrong entry without following its pointer, and the key is stored inside the value's own object. A lookup touches about two places in memory instead of four.

Redis 8 cut its own cost per key by a different route. On the lab machine, the same 100,000 keys cost 75 bytes each on Redis 7.2.4, 55 on Redis 8.10.3 and 46 on Valkey 9.1.3. A TTL, the time to live after which Redis deletes the key, added 20 to 35 bytes more.

The table also has to grow as keys arrive. Doubling a table of 10 million buckets in one go would hold the only thread for a long time. So both servers rehash, moving the entries into a bigger table, a little at a time. They keep the old and the new table side by side. Every command that touches the table moves a few buckets across, a short step on the server's background timer moves more, and lookups check both tables until the old one is empty. Redis also avoids resizing while it saves a snapshot of its data in the background, because moving memory then makes the operating system copy pages (lesson 9).

Valkey's developers kept that incremental rehashing in their new table. They also kept SCAN's cursor, a bookmark for reading the keys in pages, and the random sampling of keys that eviction, throwing keys out when memory is full, depends on (lesson 5). Those needs are why they wrote their own table instead of taking a ready-made one.

So far we've weighed keys. Next, we'll put one type to work: a ranking of shops that stays sorted as payments arrive.

try.title: Weigh a key on Redis 8.10 and on Valkey 9.1
steps: Run the script below in a terminal. It starts a throwaway Redis 8.10.3 and a throwaway Valkey 9.1.3 (the first run downloads the Valkey image, the package Docker starts it from). It writes 100,000 tiny keys into each, without and then with a TTL, prints the memory per key from used_memory, and removes both containers.
Before it prints, predict which server stores a key in fewer bytes, and how much a TTL adds.
Notice that one script talks to both servers: the Valkey image also ships redis-cli, as another name for valkey-cli.

code.title: terminal
code.html: # one throwaway server of each, then 100,000 tiny keys in each, with and without a TTL docker run --rm -d --name sfz-redis-mem -m 256m redis:8.10.3 > /dev/null docker run --rm -d --name sfz-valkey-mem -m 256m valkey/valkey:9.1.3 > /dev/null sleep 2 used() { docker exec "$1" redis-cli INFO memory | grep '^used_memory:' | tr -dc '0-9'; } for c in sfz-redis-mem sfz-valkey-mem; do for args in "" ", 'EX', 3600"; do docker exec "$c" redis-cli FLUSHALL > /dev/null before=$(used "$c") docker exec "$c" redis-cli EVAL "for i = 1, 100000 do redis.call('SET', 'idem:' .. i, 'done'$args) end return 1" 0 > /dev/null echo "$c${args:+ with TTL}: $(( ($(used "$c") - before) / 100000 )) bytes per key" done done docker rm -f sfz-redis-mem sfz-valkey-mem > /dev/null

try.expect: On the lab machine: sfz-redis-mem: 55 bytes per key, sfz-redis-mem with TTL: 79 bytes per key (84 in a second run, depending on how far Redis's table of deadlines had grown), sfz-valkey-mem: 46 bytes per key and sfz-valkey-mem with TTL: 66 bytes per key. Each key name is about 10 bytes and each value the 4-byte string done, so most of what you pay for is bookkeeping. The same script against redis:7.2.4, the version Valkey forked from, printed 75 and 108. Both servers have cut the cost per key since they split, and Valkey a little further.

refs.title: Valkey blog: A new hash table (Valkey 8.1)
Yang et al., A large scale analysis of hundreds of in-memory cache clusters at Twitter (OSDI 2020)

aside.title: Why fuss over 20 bytes a key?
aside.html: Because a store in memory has to fit all of its data in RAM, and RAM costs far more per byte than disk. Twenty bytes times 40 million keys is 800 MB, a good share of a server's memory, and it holds nothing you asked to store. When the memory runs out, Redis either refuses new writes or throws keys away, and lesson 5 covers both. So in a store that lives in memory, the bookkeeping per key is a large part of the bill.

sections.h: Ranking shops with a sorted set: scores, ties and ranks that start at 0
sections.html:
Rank 20,000 shops by approved payments, and refresh the ranking on a screen every second. In SQL, the language most databases understand, you'd ask for ORDER BY approvals DESC LIMIT 10 each time. The database would sort, or walk an index (a lookup table kept in order), on every refresh. A sorted set does the ordering when you write instead. Every ZINCRBY moves the member to its new place, so reading the top ten is reading the first ten entries.

ZINCRBY merchants:approved 1 m-17 adds one approval to shop m-17, and creates the member if it's new. ZRANGE merchants:approved 0 9 REV WITHSCORES returns the top ten with their scores, highest first (REV reverses the usual low-to-high order). ZREVRANK merchants:approved m-17 returns the shop's place, counted from the top.

Three details cause most ranking bugs.

Ranks start at 0. ZREVRANK returns 0 for the leader, so add one before a person sees it.

Ties are ordered by member, byte by byte. In ascending order, m-anna comes before m-bert when both have 5. REV flips the whole order, ties included, so m-bert comes first. If the product wants "whoever got there first wins the tie", the member name can't give you that. You have to fold the time into the score (see Go deeper).

Scores are doubles, 64-bit numbers with a decimal point. Whole numbers are exact up to 2^53 (2 to the power 53), about 9 × 10^15, which is plenty for counts and for amounts in cents. Fractions aren't always exact, so store cents, never euros with decimals.

Since Redis 6.2, ZRANGE takes REV, BYSCORE, BYLEX and LIMIT, and the docs mark the older ZREVRANGE and ZRANGEBYSCORE as deprecated: still there, but on the way out. Since 7.2, ZRANK and ZREVRANK accept WITHSCORE and return the rank and the score in one round trip. Under the hood, with the encodings from earlier, ZSCORE asks the hash table, which is O(1). ZADD, ZREVRANK and ZRANGE walk the skip list: O(log N), plus M for the members a range returns. In Jedis, a Tuple holds one member and its score, and a KeyValue holds a rank and a score:

Java
List<Tuple> top = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 9).rev());
KeyValue<Long, Double> me = redis.zrevrankWithScore("merchants:approved", "m-17");   // null if absent
Kotlin
val top: List<Tuple> = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 9).rev())
val me: KeyValue<Long, Double>? = redis.zrevrankWithScore("merchants:approved", "m-17")   // null if absent

A ranking like this stays cheap while each key is small. Next, we'll see what happens when a key keeps growing.

try.title: Rank four shops, two of them tied
steps: Add four shops with the first command. m-anna and m-bert both have 5.
Predict the order of the two ZRANGE calls before you run them, ties included.
Run the rest. What rank does m-anna have, and does it count from 0 or 1?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
ZADD merchants:today 5 m-anna 5 m-bert 7 m-cora 3 m-dave
ZRANGE merchants:today 0 -1 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE merchants:today 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
ZREVRANK merchants:today m-anna WITHSCORE
ZINCRBY merchants:today 1 m-anna
ZRANGE merchants:today 0 2 REV WITHSCORES
ZREVRANK merchants:today m-zed

try.expect: Ascending, the order is m-dave 3, m-anna 5, m-bert 5, m-cora 7: the tie goes to the smaller member name. With REV it's m-cora, m-bert, m-anna, m-dave, so the tie flips too. ZREVRANK ... WITHSCORE returns 1) (integer) 2 and 2) "5", so m-anna is third, counted from 0. After ZINCRBY, it has "6", and the top three are m-cora 7, m-anna 6, m-bert 5. A member that doesn't exist gets (nil), Redis's word for no value.

sections.h: One big key can make every client wait
sections.html:
Put the one thread from Inside an in-memory store next to this lesson's Big-O table, and you get the most common way a Redis server stops answering. An O(N) command on a key with a big N holds the only thread for as long as it runs. Nobody writes a slow SMEMBERS on purpose. A set of flagged cards starts with 50 members, grows for two years, and one day holds a million. The code that reads it in one call never changed.

On the lab server, a set of a million card ids took about 30 MB. Reading it whole with SMEMBERS held the one thread for about 54 ms, and freeing it with DEL took about 40 ms. For those milliseconds, every other client of that Redis waited. Run the same read from a few copies of the program at once, and the waits add up. A key that large is called a big key, and the cure is to stop it growing, or to touch it only in small pieces.

Four habits keep you out of trouble:

  • Read big collections in pages, with a cursor: SSCAN, HSCAN, ZSCAN, and SCAN for the whole keyspace. Each call returns a small batch plus a cursor to continue from. So each call does a limited amount of work, and other clients get their turn in between. For sorted sets, ZRANGE with small ranges does the same.
  • Delete big keys with UNLINK. It removes the key at once, and a background thread, bio_lazy_free, frees the memory while commands keep running.
  • Split by something natural: one set per day, one hash per shop, one sorted set per region. Ten keys of 100,000 members are kinder to everyone than one key of a million.
  • Find big keys before they find you, with MEMORY USAGE key and redis-cli --bigkeys, which walks the keyspace with SCAN.

The encoding limits give you a second reason to keep keys small: below them, the same data takes a fraction of the memory. A key you can't read in one go is too big. Split it before it grows.

Small keys still hold exact data, though, and some questions don't need exact answers. The next lesson trades exactness for memory on purpose.

try.title: Build a big key and time it
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run the first three commands. The EVAL builds a set of a million card ids. It takes most of a second, and blocks the server the whole time.
In a second terminal, read the whole set once and throw the output away: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli SMEMBERS flagged:cards > /dev/null.
Back at the prompt, run the rest: build a copy, delete one set with DEL and the other with UNLINK, then read the slow log, Redis's list of slow commands. Predict which commands it lists.
Clean up afterwards with FLUSHALL, which deletes every key, if you like. This is your own lab server.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SLOWLOG RESET
EVAL "for i = 1, 1000000 do redis.call('SADD', KEYS[1], 'card:' .. i) end return redis.call('SCARD', KEYS[1])" 1 flagged:cards
MEMORY USAGE flagged:cards
EVAL "for i = 1, 1000000 do redis.call('SADD', KEYS[1], 'card:' .. i) end return 1" 1 flagged:copy
DEL flagged:cards
UNLINK flagged:copy
SLOWLOG GET 5

try.expect: The slow log lists commands that ran longer than 10 ms. Each entry starts with an id, a Unix timestamp (seconds since 1970), the duration in microseconds and the command. On the lab server: both EVALs about 640,000 µs, SMEMBERS about 54,000 µs, and DEL about 40,000 µs. UNLINK is missing, because it returned in well under 10 ms and left the freeing to the background thread. Your numbers depend on your CPU. MEMORY USAGE printed about 37 MB: it samples a few members and multiplies up, so treat it as a rough size.

refs.title: Diagnosing latency issues (big keys and slow commands)

opening:
Picture a café owner who keeps her regulars on one notebook page. With a hundred names, the page is perfect: one sheet, and a finger finds anyone in seconds. At a few thousand, she switches to a box of index cards and a ranked list on the wall. Lookups are quick again, but the paper has grown far faster than the names.

Redis, a program that keeps data in memory and answers requests over the network, makes the same switch inside a key. A sorted set of 128 shops takes about 1 KB, and the 129th shop makes it about 11 KB. It's natural to expect a few bytes more per item. In memory, though, the bookkeeping around small items often weighs more than the items.

Inside an in-memory store showed one thread running every command, so each command's cost is everyone's. In this lesson, we'll pick a type for each job in the payments app, watch a key change shape, weigh what a key costs, and rank shops. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café owner whose notebook page turned into a box of cards. Redis makes that switch inside a key, at 128 or 512 items, and the same data can then take ten times the memory. A key that keeps growing can also hold up every client.

With the lab server running, try docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli --bigkeys from the labs folder. Then look at each key name in this lesson and ask: can it grow without limit?

Next, we'll meet structures that answer one narrow question, such as how many different cards paid today, in a small, fixed amount of memory. Some of them give up exactness to do it.

compare.title: The ranking's top N in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Leaderboard.java
java.html: public record Standing(String merchant, long approvals, long rank) {} public List<Standing> top(int n) { List<Tuple> rows = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, n - 1).rev()); List<Standing> out = new ArrayList<>(rows.size()); for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) { Tuple t = rows.get(i); out.add(new Standing(t.getElement(), (long) t.getScore(), i + 1)); // ranks start at 1 for people } return out; }

kotlin.title: Leaderboard.kt
kotlin.html: data class Standing(val merchant: String, val approvals: Long, val rank: Long) fun top(n: Int): List<Standing> = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, n - 1).rev()) .mapIndexed { i, t -> Standing(t.element, t.score.toLong(), i + 1L) } // ranks start at 1 for people

compare.note: The Redis call is the same in both: one ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES. Kotlin reads Jedis's getters as properties (t.element, t.score), and a data class replaces the Java record, a small class that only holds values. Watch for missing values where the two languages meet. zrevrank returns a Java Long that is null when the shop has no entry, and Kotlin can't tell from Java code whether a value may be null (it calls such a value a platform type). Declare it Long?, so the compiler makes you handle the null. Pass it unchecked to code that wants a Long, and you get a NullPointerException the first time a shop has no entry.

worked.title: Keep a sorted set per shop small on purpose

steps.say: The fraud team wants a screen that shows, for each shop, the card BINs with the most declined payments this hour. A BIN is the first six digits of a card number, and it names the bank that gave out the card. A sorted set per shop and hour fits: the member is the BIN, and the score counts the declines. About 20,000 shops are active in an hour, and a busy one sees declines from 300 different BINs.
steps.code: String key = "declines:" + merchant + ":h" + hour; // declines:m-17:h14 redis.zincrby(key, 1, bin);

alt.html: val key = "declines:$merchant:h$hour" // declines:m-17:h14 redis.zincrby(key, 1.0, bin)

steps.say: Size it before you ship it. 300 members is past zset-max-listpack-entries, so a busy shop's key is a skip list. On the lab server, a 300-BIN set took 25,223 bytes, and a 100-BIN set took 730 bytes as a listpack (short members made of digits pack tightly). Across 20,000 shops, that's about 500 MB against about 15 MB.

The screen shows the top 20. So keep the 100 highest and drop the rest after every increment. The key never passes 101 members, and stays a listpack. A BIN that falls off and comes back starts again from 1, which is fine for a "most declines" view. Trimming a key that's already a skip list wouldn't help: it stays a skip list.
steps.code: redis.zincrby(key, 1, bin); redis.zremrangeByRank(key, 0, -101); // keep the 100 highest; the key never passes 101 members

alt.html: redis.zincrby(key, 1.0, bin) redis.zremrangeByRank(key, 0, -101) // keep the 100 highest; the key never passes 101 members

steps.say: Read the top 20 with one ZRANGE, and give the key a lifetime so that old hours clean themselves up (Expiry, eviction and memory, lesson 5). These are two separate commands per decline, so another client can run between them. Here that only means the trim runs a moment late. Serial execution, in the Transactions track, shows how to make increment-and-trim one atomic step with a script.
steps.code: List<Tuple> top20 = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 19).rev()); redis.expire(key, 7_200); // two hours, then Redis deletes the key

alt.html: val top20 = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 19).rev()) redis.expire(key, 7_200) // two hours, then Redis deletes the key

lab.title: Catch the encoding switch, then build a ranking of shops
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. All 14 fail. They run against a shared Redis 8.10 container, which Testcontainers, a library for tests, starts for you. Each test gets its own key prefix, a start for its key names, so the tests don't collide.
In EncodingProbe.java, write describe with objectEncoding and memoryUsage, Jedis's names for OBJECT ENCODING and MEMORY USAGE.

Write growUntilConverted. Add element 1 and describe the key, then loop from 2 to maxSize: add, describe, and return a Transition as soon as the encoding changes. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l03.EncodingProbeTest'. Its tests pin the 8.10 defaults: 129 for sorted sets and sets of strings, 513 for hashes and sets of whole numbers, and one long member converting at once.
In Leaderboard.kt, write record with zincrby, and top with one zrangeWithScores call using ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, n - 1).rev(). Turn positions counted from 0 into ranks that start at 1.
Write standingOf with zrevrankWithScore, and around with zrevrank and one range around that rank. Run all the tests.
hints: OBJECT ENCODING comes back as a lowercase String. Compare encodings with equals, not ==.
zrevrankWithScore returns a KeyValue<Long, Double>: key is the rank counted from 0, and value is the score. It's null when the shop has no entry.
In around, the range starts at max(0, rank - radius). You don't need to limit the end: ZRANGE stops at the last member.
Scores are doubles. toLong() is safe here, because the totals are whole numbers far below 2^53.

drill.title: Top five and a rank, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the Jedis calls for two questions about merchants:approved. First, print the top 5 shops with their totals, highest first, numbered from 1. Second, get the rank of m-17 counted from 1, or null if it has no entry. Then compare. Did you remember that ranks start at 0?

answer.html: List<Tuple> top5 = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 4).rev()); for (int i = 0; i < top5.size(); i++) { System.out.printf("%d. %s %d%n", i + 1, top5.get(i).getElement(), (long) top5.get(i).getScore()); } Long rank = redis.zrevrank("merchants:approved", "m-17"); // 0-based, null if absent Long shown = rank == null ? null : rank + 1;

alt.html: val top5 = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 4).rev()) top5.forEachIndexed { i, t -> println("${i + 1}. ${t.element} ${t.score.toLong()}") } val rank: Long? = redis.zrevrank("merchants:approved", "m-17") // 0-based, null if absent val shown = rank?.plus(1)

recap: Five types cover most jobs: strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets. Choose by the operation you need, then check its cost in Big-O.

Small hashes, sets and sorted sets are listpacks, and small sets of whole numbers are intsets. Past 128 or 512 entries, or one value over 64 bytes, Redis converts them to hash tables or skip lists, and never converts back.
The conversion costs memory: on the lab server, a 128-member sorted set took about 1 KB, and the 129-member one about 11 KB.

All the keys live in one big hash table, so every key carries fixed bookkeeping. A tiny key cost about 75 bytes on Redis 7.2.4, 55 on Redis 8.10 and 46 on Valkey 9.1, whose 8.1 release moved to buckets the size of one CPU load.
Sorted sets order by score, then by member bytes, and REV flips both. Ranks start at 0. Scores are doubles, exact for whole numbers up to 2^53.
The limit: a big key makes O(N) commands block everyone. Read it in pages with the SCAN family, delete it with UNLINK, and split keys by day, shop or region.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why MEMORY USAGE of their sorted set jumped from about 1 KB to about 11 KB when it went from 128 to 129 members, and whether deleting members will bring it back down. Explain.
explain.answer: Up to 128 members, the default zset-max-listpack-entries, Redis stores a sorted set as a listpack. That's one block of memory with the entries packed back to back, no pointers, searched from the start, which is cheap for a small set. The 129th member makes Redis convert the key to the general form: a hash table from member to score, plus a skip list in score order. Every member now has its own pieces of memory, pointers and a slot in the hash table, so the same data takes about ten times the memory. In exchange, finding a score takes O(1) and finding a rank O(log N), instead of a walk through the block. Deleting members won't bring it back, because Redis only converts upward. If we want the compact form, we have to keep the key under 128 members from the start, for example by trimming after each insert, or rebuild it into a new key.

deeper.html:
Two pieces of old advice are out of date. Old posts put the embstr cut-off at 44 bytes. In Redis 8.10, a 44-byte value under a 1-character key came out raw, and so did a 35-byte value under a 41-character key, because the cut-off now depends on the key's length as well. Old posts also say ziplist. Redis 7.0 replaced ziplist with listpack, and the old *-ziplist-* setting names still work as other names for the new ones.

To break ties by time, fold the time into the score. Say the product wants the shop that reached a total first to rank higher. Use score = approvals × 100,000 + (99,999 − second of the day). A day has 86,400 seconds, so the time part fits in five digits, and a higher total always wins. Between equal totals, the earlier second gives the bigger score. Doubles stay exact up to 2^53, so totals up to about 90 billion are safe. The catch: every new approval must rewrite the time part too, which is read, compute and write. Two clients can interleave that, so do it in a Lua script (Serial execution, in the Transactions track), or accept small errors.

The value limits count bytes, not characters. In UTF-8, the usual way to store text as bytes, an accented letter such as é takes two bytes. So a 40-character shop name full of them can cross the 64-byte zset-max-listpack-value.

The limits decide how much a whole server holds, too. A million payment hashes of 12 fields each stay listpacks, and take a fraction of the memory that a million 600-field hashes would.

Raising the limits is allowed. CONFIG SET zset-max-listpack-entries 256 keeps bigger sets compact, at the cost of O(N) inserts and lookups on longer blocks. The defaults are a sensible trade, so measure before you change them. Existing keys aren't converted when you change the setting; it applies the next time a key would grow.

Redis keeps squeezing the big encodings too. The 8.6 release notes list a large memory cut for hashes in a hash table and sorted sets in a skip list. Redis 8.10 added a new layout for many hashes that share the same field names, loaded with HIMPORT. Plain HSET keys, like the ones in this lesson's lab, still show listpack and hashtable.

Valkey's write-up of its new table explains why it didn't adopt a ready-made design such as a Swiss table, a fast hash table design from Google. The keyspace has to support incremental rehashing, a SCAN cursor that survives a resize, and picking random keys for eviction and for expiry, and ready-made tables offer none of that. The developers report that speed changed very little either way. The win was memory: roughly 20 bytes per key, and 30 per key with a TTL, against the old layout, plus 10 to 20 bytes per item inside big hashes, sets and sorted sets.
